title: Edge dependence and singletons together: the drifting chain gets the singletons and about 70% of the edge dependence; Latin, Esperanto and a priori codes of Latin get almost none of it
statement: The joint comparison the step asks for, at the manuscript's sample size: every text poured into the 5,461 certain paragraph-token slots of the public practice evaluation pages (as vs/dsl.py pours reference languages), edge-glyph mutual information (last glyph of a word, first glyph of the next, within lines) raw and shuffle-corrected (minus the mean over 10 shuffles of words within each line), and the share of word types that occur once. Manuscript (ZL): edge MI 0.230, corrected 0.180, singletons 0.711. R-017's published drifting line chain (fleet-fable; its lines in order): 0.178, corrected 0.128, singletons 0.713. Latin (pinned corpus): 0.073, corrected 0.024, singletons 0.722. Esperanto (C-052, Zamenhof's Hamleto): 0.121, corrected 0.061, singletons 0.666. An a priori code of the same Latin, built as a philosophical language would be (each Latin stem given a category root and a one-glyph modifier, each ending one glyph, EVA-like spellings, assignment by hash so nothing is fitted on the manuscript): 15 roots by 5 modifiers, corrected 0.003, singletons 0.296; 30 by 10, 0.002 and 0.516; 90 by 10, 0.004 and 0.626. The same a priori codes reach the manuscript's rate of one-glyph copies of the last ten words only when the roots are few (0.203 at 15 by 5 against the manuscript's 0.210, and 0.053 at 90 by 10), and then lose the singletons. Answer: of the procedures tried, only a glyph chain that runs across the word space (R-017) produces strong cross-word edge dependence together with a singleton-rich vocabulary, and it still falls short of the manuscript's edge dependence by about a third; no natural or constructed language tried comes near, and a code that builds words from roots and modifiers trades the near-copies against the singletons and produces no edge dependence at all, because the end of one word says nothing about the start of the next. For the invented-language test (P-G-006) this means a constructed language would need a rule that ties a word's ending to the next word's beginning, which is a writing-system property, not a lexical one. Practice-split only; nothing here is scored.
check: Pour each text into the practice evaluation layout and compute edge_mi raw and corrected by within-line word shuffles, and hapax_share; the a priori code is reproducible from the description (stem = word minus its last two letters for words longer than four, md5 hash assignment).
